items.title: Read spatial and time wave records
items.student: Supplied transverse-wave profile at one instant:crests at x0.20,1.00,1.80m with displacement+0.030m;trough displacement−0.030m;equilibrium0. A fixed point has successive crests at t0,0.25,0.50s. Draw a labelled spatial profile and a separate displacement-time sketch. Find amplitude,peak-to-peak displacement,wavelength,period and frequency. Explain why a spatial crest separation and a time between crests have different units. Contrast transverse displacement with longitudinal sound compressions in air.
items.teacher: Amplitude0.030m,peak-to-peak0.060m,λ0.80m,T0.25s,f4Hz. Space graph xaxisdistance;time graph xaxistime. Sound in air is longitudinal particle oscillation parallel to propagation;transverse profile is a representation of a different oscillation direction,not literal up/down sound particles. Wave transport transfers energy,not every particle travelling with the wave.

items.title: Interpret v=fλ rather than recite it
items.student: A periodic wave advances one wavelength during one period. Explain v=λ/T=fλ using distance/time and f=1/T. For a model with v12m/s,f3Hz,findλ andT. If frequency becomes6Hz while speed in the same nondispersive model stays12m/s,find newλ/T. Explain why doubling frequency need not double speed and why amplitude is absent from this linear relation.
items.teacher: Initialλ4m,T1/3≈0.333s;newλ2m,T1/6≈0.167s. Fixedmedium/model speed gives inverse frequency-wavelength relation. Amplitude not in this linear wave-speed equation;do not generalise to all nonlinear/dispersive contexts. Symbol v is propagation speed here,not particle oscillation velocity.

items.title: Wave-equation calculations and units
items.student: For supplied models calculate:A speed fromf50Hz,λ0.40m;Bfrequencyfromv340m/s,λ0.85m;C wavelengthfromv300m/s,f1.5kHz;Dperiodfromf25Hz. Convert kHz toHz andshowunits/rearrangement. Explain why using1.5 directly in C gives a thousand-fold error. None is an actual measured wave.
items.teacher: A20m/s;B400Hz;C1500Hz→0.20m;D0.040s. Checkv=fλ andT=1/f dimensionally. Speed/wavelength values are task-specific conditions,not universal for all sound. Do not identify an unknown medium from these numbers alone.

items.title: A boundary can change speed and wavelength
items.student: Supplied periodic source frequency5Hz;wave speed20m/s in mediumA and10m/s in mediumB. Assuming stationary boundary and unchanged source frequency,calculate wavelengths and periods in both. Draw schematic equally timed wavefronts with closer spacing inB. Explain which properties change and why frequency stays fixed. Refraction means direction changes when entering obliquely under suitable speed change;normal incidence can change speed/λ without bending.
items.teacher: λA4m,λB2m,T0.20s both,f5Hz both. Frequency remains source-driven in this stationary model. Do not preserveλ while changingv at fixedf. Slower medium bends an oblique ray towardnormal;not every boundary requires bending atnormalincidence. No specific real medium or measurement inferred.

items.title: Reflection with a defined normal
items.student: Draw a flat reflecting surface and a normal at the incident point. A ray makes35° with the normal;draw and label the reflected ray and both angles. Compare reflection of light in a mirror with sound echo at a wall. Explain that incident/reflected angles are measured from the normal,not surface,and ideal reflection stays in the original medium. No laser or mirror-glare experiment.
items.teacher: Reflection angle35° from normal,55° from surface;incident/reflected rays opposite sides ofnormal in sameplane. Reflection changes propagation direction,not necessarily sourcefrequency. Mirrors/light and walls/sound share a model but materials/absorption/scattering differ. A diagram is not an actual demonstration.

items.title: Echo method with an actual-action boundary
items.student: Conditional actual observation:teacher selects a quiet,approved level area away from roads/traffic/hearing-sensitive activity,with a suitable distant reflecting wall and safe standing zone. Use one moderate hand clap,not amplified sound,shouting,impulses near ears or repeated noise escalation. Record whether a distinct delayed echo is heard;an absent/unclear echo is a valid observation,not permission to get louder. Assign actual source/listener/recorder roles and record site/date/conditions. If no approved suitable site,use supplied records and mark not performed. Supplied fictional echo round-trip time0.40s with sound speed340m/s:find wall distance. Compare a second record wall17m away:find round-trip time. Explain why reverberation in a small room may not be a separately resolved echo and why ordinary reaction timing cannot precisely measure such short delays. No actual speed/distance is prefilled.
items.teacher: d340×0.40/2=68m;for17m,t2×17/340=0.10s. Out-and-back path gives factor2. Actual quiet-site approval/roles/heard-or-not record needed for demonstration;paper values are not fieldmeasurements. Multiple close reflections can blur into reverberation;no precisionclaim fromhumanreactiontiming. Stopratherthanraiselevel if conditionsunsuitable.

items.title: Sound refraction:day/night is a conditional model
items.student: Supplied temperature-only profiles,ignoring wind: D has warmer ground air and cooler air above; N has cooler ground air with a warmer layer above. Sound travels faster in warmer air. Draw height diagrams with speed-gradient labels and initially near-horizontal rays; predict bending in each and explain possible ground-audibility differences. Qualify the common day/night association: clock time or one listening report does not establish gradients,wind,humidity or audibility. Reference:Penn State Acoustics,https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/demos/refract/refract.html. Optional approved video needs teacher provision and an actual viewing record; diagrams are not a watched clip.
items.teacher: D:speed decreases with height,rays curve upward toward the slower region. N:speed increases with height,rays curve down toward cooler,slower ground air. These profiles may occur on sunny days or clear nights,but not always. Wind,terrain,source/receiver height and background noise also matter. No universal night-audibility law or local weather measurement follows. Gradient bending differs from a surface-reflection bounce.

items.title: Diffraction depends on relative scale
items.student: Gap0.50m;sound A wavelength0.85m,B0.085m. Calculate wavelength/gap ratios and predict which tends to spread more in this simplified geometry. Draw spreading wavefronts. Distinguish diffraction around edges from reflection at surfaces and refraction due to speed variation. Explain why visible light,with wavelength far smaller than a doorway,usually shows much less obvious doorway spreading than ordinary sound.
items.teacher: Ratios1.7 and0.17;A tends to show stronger spreading when wavelength is comparable to opening size. Diffraction is not restricted to exact equality,and all waves can diffract under suitable conditions. Exact patterns need geometry. Distinguish edge spreading from bouncing or speed-gradient bending.

items.title: Around-corner sound investigation
items.student: Conditional approved observation:in a quiet supervised school area,a speaker uses a low conversational voice while a listener stands safely around an approved corner,out of direct view. Do not block corridors,enter traffic,shout,use earphones or increase volume. Record positions,heard/not heard,conditions,date and actual roles. Repeat a small safe position change only with permission. If unsuitable,use this supplied fictional record:voice audible out of view near a doorway,with hard walls present. Explain possible diffraction and reflected alternatives;draw both paths. A single observation does not isolate diffraction. Mark actual experiment not performed when using only the record.
items.teacher: Sound can diffract around edges and reflect from walls. Audibility alone cannot isolate one cause;stronger inference needs controlled geometry/source conditions. Avoid precision or loudness comparisons without measurement. Actual safe observation demonstrates an effect with limits;print records do not certify source actions.

items.title: Environmental wave cases and source distinctions
items.student: Supplied cases:coastal water waves can move sediment and erode or reshape shores,affecting habitats,communities,infrastructure and port operations. Underwater human-generated sound from ships/construction can affect marine-animal communication or behaviour depending on level,frequency,duration and species. Distinguish water-surface waves from acoustic waves. Explain possible benefits/harms and two missing local facts. No visit or measured local impact is claimed. References:NOAA OceanService,https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/wavesinocean.html;NOAA Fisheries,https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/national/science-data/ocean-noise.
items.teacher: These are different wave phenomena. Coastal sediment movement can be natural and its effects depend on location. Underwater acoustic exposure differs from surface-water motion;not all ship sound causes injury. Need site,exposure,species/habitat,conditions and baseline evidence. Supplied summaries are not local measurements.

items.title: Mitigation needs evidence and trade-offs
items.student: Fictional options:A restrict access to an already identified unsafe shore during official warnings;B install an engineered breakwater without study;C reduce avoidable shipping noise through qualified planning. Match each to water-wave/acoustic cases. Explain why B needs engineering/ecological assessment and C has no quantified benefit from a general summary. Request evidence covering communities,marine ecosystems,infrastructure and operations. No construction,marine visit or emergency activity occurs.
items.teacher: A reduces exposure to identified water-wave hazards under local official guidance. B needs qualified design and sediment,habitat and navigation trade-off assessment. C targets some human-generated acoustic exposure with operational/ecological constraints. Request local risk,exposure,habitat,infrastructure and operation data and community input. No invented percentage or universal best mitigation.

items.title: Waves and safer road-use reasoning
items.student: Supplied cards:rear-view mirrors reflect light;optical lenses refract light;horn/siren sound can diffract around edges and also reflect. Explain a use and limit for each. Correct:hearing around a corner proves the road clear,and any mirror removes every blind spot. Draw a relevant model and identify evidence needed before real decisions. No road visit,vehicle operation,laser or loud sound. Explain how wave knowledge helps while proper road procedures and attention remain necessary.
items.teacher: Mirrors aid viewing but geometry and blind spots remain. Lenses support focusing under appropriate design conditions. Diffraction may permit hearing hidden sources,but neither direction/distance nor absence of sound guarantees a clear road. Models are not traffic detectors;no actual field demonstration,safety certification or legal rule is inferred.

items.title: Final-only wave record
items.student: HELD-OUT FINAL. All values/models supplied:spatial crests x0.10,0.70,1.30m,displacement±0.020m;fixed-point successive crests t0,0.20,0.40s. Boundary source frequency10Hz,speeds30m/s in A and20m/s in B. Echo round-trip time0.30s,sound340m/s. Profile:warmer ground,cooler air above,wind ignored. Gap0.40m,wavelength0.80m. A fictional voice is heard out of view near hard walls;no actual class record. Environmental cases:underwater human-generated noise and coastal wave erosion,without site/exposure assessment. Road card:mirror light reflection,not a road test. Equations:v=fλ,T=1/f,echo distance=vt/2. No actual experiment,video,environmental measurement or traffic activity supplied.
items.teacher: I1:amplitude0.020m,peak-to-peak0.040m,wavelength0.60m,period0.20s,frequency5Hz,speed3m/s. Boundary wavelengths3m/2m,period0.10s,frequency10Hz both. Echo51m. I2:warm-ground profile bends upward toward cooler/slower air;wavelength/gap2 supports substantial spreading,while walls may also reflect. No single-cause proof. I3:mirror benefit/limit,water-wave versus acoustic impacts and evidence requests. Actual demonstrations remain separately observed requirements,not written-model credit.
